speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my privilege as Minister of Veterans Affairs to remind all members and all Canadians that tomorrow, November 11, is Remembrance Day.
Well over half of our present population was born after the end of the Second World War, and, as the echoes of that conflict become fainter, there is always a possibility that, for the younger generations, November 11 will have no special significance. I consider this would be a tragedy because there is an inspirational story rooted in our past.
The day before yesterday I was at Vimy Ridge, where Canadians won everlasting glory. On that occasion one could not help but be reminded of the words of General Byng, the commander of our forces at Vimy, who said:
There they stood on Vimy Ridge on the ninth day of April, 1917, men from Quebec stood shoulder to shoulder with men from British Columbia and Alberta and there was forged a nation tempered by the fires of sacrifice and hammered on the anvil of high adventure.
Over 600,000 Canadians fought in the First World War. They were so splendid at the Battle of the Somme that British Prime Minister David Lloyd George later wrote:
The Canadians played a part of such distinction that henceforward they were marked out as storm troops; for the remainder of the war they were brought along to head the assault in one great battle after another. Whenever the Germans found the Canadian corps coming into the line they prepared for the worst.
Next summer we will be commemorating the fortieth anniversary of Dieppe, where Canadians were also asked to serve as storm troops. Those men who landed on the Normandy beaches were in the finest traditions of the Canadian forces, as were our airmen in the Battle of Britain, and our seamen who crewed the perilous convoys of the North Atlantic.
This tradition of service and sacrifice was continued in the Korean war when Canadians volunteered to join the United Nations peace foice.
Tomorrow, November 11, we will be remembering those men and women from all those wars who gave up their lives so others could be free, and at the same time we will be recognizing the achievements of former members of our forces.
For the millions of our young people who have known nothing but the privilege of peace, let us hope that Remembrance Day will always be something special. If we take the
time to reflect on the example set by our forebears, Canadians can face the future with confidence.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, they served; we care.
On behalf of the Conservative Party I wish to add our thoughts of remembrance at this time of reflection. So basic was the belief that everyone has a right to the freedoms we now cherish that over 100,000 Canadian men and women gave their very lives to ensure that end. Through the World Wars, the Korean war, and many other battles, hundreds of thousands of Canadians have fought to ensure that these cherished freedoms would never be forfeited. We gratefully remember their sacrifice.
November 11 will mark the passage of another year since the fighting ceased on the western front. Then, as now, mankind prayed that the last war had been waged. Whenever Canadians have been needed, they have served and served with distinction. Many returned maimed and disabled. We hope there will be amendments to the Human Rights Act to bring equality to the handicapped in this International Year of Disabled Persons.
I feel it is our responsibility, as the benefactors of their arduous labours, to remember both the 100,000 war dead and the 770,000 veterans who now live on. They deserve to be treated with respect and compassion. Currently many veterans die before they receive their due benefits from the country for which they have faithfully done battle.
It is an honour to remember our fallen comrades through eulogy, but we should also remember the actions of our living veterans by acting ourselves. The greatest tribute we could give them would be to eliminate by next Remembrance Day any causes of frustration they may now have and, in particular, the excessive time delays in processing pension applications. They served; we remember.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I lived in Great Britain during the Second World War. I remember the Second World War as a boy, the air raid sirens, the nights in the bomb shelters, the enemy aircraft overhead, the terror of the bombs, and I remember the devastation.
I remember when it ended, when men and women returned
from the battle front; some walked and some could not, and we
thought of those who had died protecting us, and we vowed

November 10, 1981
that never again would this occur. With the faces of lost loved ones still fresh in our minds we determined that we would remember them.
We owed a great deal to those whose lifetime would be one of suffering, and we owed a great deal to the widows and families of those who had lost their lives. We were prepared to make sacrifices then to ensure that they would never want. Have we kept the faith? Could we have done better? Have we truly remembered as we promised that we would?
On behalf of Stanley Knowles, whose battle for veterans has been and continues to be unended, and on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, I join in paying tribute and pledging that in the year ahead we will strive to meet our debt to those who served our country in World Wars I and II, in Korea, and in the other conflicts as part of our peacekeeping effort, conflicts in which we participated willingly. And I pray we will remain mindful of the need to develop throughout the world an economic order that will eliminate poverty and want for all people, and to that end eliminate the need for war.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday the Canadian Labour Congress properly pointed out to many members of this House that our country is currently losing more than 70 million working days a year because of work accidents and illnesses. That is fully six times the annual loss due to walk-outs and strikes. In the typical year about 20,000 Canadians are permanently disabled and more than a thousand are killed while on the job. I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie):
That this House calls on the government to amend Part IV of the Canada Labour Code as quickly as possible in order to deal more effectively with the prevention of workplace accidents and diseases, and to streamline existing procedures under which fully 15 separate federal departments and agencies currently have an involvement in occupational health and safety.

As an expression of continuing non-partisan concern with this issue, and in view of the seriousness of it for the native people of Canada, would the Prime Minister agree that it would be an important step for a letter to be sent, signed by the Prime Minister and the leaders of the other opposition parties in the House of Commons, to

Madam Speaker, the hon. member says that all parties in the House of Commons agree that that should be in. I am not quite certain that has been the case over the past year. 1 wonder why the hon. member would want me to write that letter only on behalf of the aboriginals and not on behalf of all other Canadians who do not have the equality clause and legality clause entrenched, that are subject to "notwithstanding." Yesterday we heard about women's rights, and I am sure we will hear about the disabled and so on.
I am trying to get the hon. member to understand that there was an accord last Thursday. It left some things out that we did not like left out. speechtext: Can the minister tell us why the American firm was selected since his own tender specifications and the briefings of his officials firmly stated, as early as 1979, that no foreign company would be allowed to bid? Can the minister further tell us what plans he has to compensate those six Canadian companies, several of which are in my constituency? They followed our rules, they bid legitimately, and each one of them spent thousands of dollars in the course of losing in this bidding process.

subtopic: CONTRACT TO OPERATE DUTY FREE STORES AT TORONTO INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I doubt very much if foreign companies were prevented from bidding in the first place, because a number of them did. What happened was that when this was found, and when
November 10, 1981

one of the foreign bidders appeared to be the winner, a decision was made to get the case to FIRA.
FIRA and my department developed a regime for duty-free shops. The regime indicates, for example, that the shares should be owned more than 51 per cent by Canadians, that the directors, except one, should be Canadian, that employees should be Canadian, that preference should be given to Canadian goods, etc. A regime was developed which is met by the company which now has the contract. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour. Yesterday representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress, when attending a convention discussing health and safety regulations, met with several Members of Parliament asking for more uniform and stronger legislation in the health and safety field. Will the minister advise the House if he is giving consideration to amending the Canada Labour Code to implement these recommendations, and, particularly, if he is considering the establishment of federal minimum standards to protect the health and safety of all Canadian workers?

subtopic: FEDERAL STANDARDS TO PROTECT HEALTH AND SAFETY OF WORKERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, submissions have been made to the Government of Canada by interested individuals, by labour organizations, and by employer groups. Those recommendations have been looked into very carefully, and those recommendations that are constructive and positive will Find their expression in a proposed measure that hopefully will be introduced in the House in the new year. This government introduced the labour code just a few years ago, and it will be this Liberal government that will continue on the road leading to better protection of the Canadian worker, hopefully with the support of all members in this House.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, having given you notice of a question of privilege I wish to bring to your attention and request your guidance on a matter which brings into disrepute the integrity of this House.
My question of privilege arises from a householder printed by the House of Commons on House of Commons stationery and paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. I refer to this householder in my hand which I have no way of identifying. I have no idea of the constituency involved or which member will be using this householder to communicate with his or her constituents. There were several thousands of these in a truck in the basement of the Confederation Building. The only thing I can go by is that on that truck there was the name of the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), a member of the NDP.
This booklet contains the biographies of members of the NDP from Saskatchewan only, plus a quote from J. S. Woods-worth. I am not sure what he has to do with the present NDP. He was the leader of the CCF.
The cover is headed "Our West". I would draw to your attention page 3, headed "By way of Introduction". In the second paragraph this appears:
-even though some of you don't live in constituencies represented by a New Democrat... You are welcome to contact any one of us at anytime-
I feel that this is a misuse of taxpayers' funds to publish something that could better be done by party headquarters, and in most parties it is done that way. This is a political handout.
I would just like to read from a page of Hansard where Your Honour made a ruling in reply to a question on which I had asked you to give some guidance. At page 5325 of Hansard for December 4, 1980, you are recorded as stating:
There are rules regulating the contents of the householder mailings, but members must take full responsibility for material mailed under their frank and written on official stationery.
Those rules which you referred to and which we in this House, I would hope, would all attempt to follow include the rule under the Allowances and Services Printing Guidelines. In Section 6-5(b) it states in part:
-a political, partisan or party nature-
Anything in that category is unacceptable. I think when you look at this purported householder you will find it is of a political and partisan nature. Also under Section 6-5 (b), referring to unacceptable printing requests, we find:
(iv) election campaign material-
I would suggest this would fall into that class. It includes:
(v) publications normally made available by party headquarters.
I would also like to draw to your attention a document sent to all members regarding household mailings received in my office on October 8, sent on October 7, 1981. On the back page it states in part:
-the purpose of the four householder mailings available at Parliamentary expense is to enable Members to convey information to their constituents-
It says, Madam Speaker, "convey information to their constituents".
When I look at this mailer, Madam Speaker, I do not find which constituency it would go to. I do not see anything different in it that we and all political parties would ordinarily send out from our political headquarters. I do not see anything in it that would make me think it is anything different from a political publication.
The people of Canada support all of us equally in this House in our efforts to communicate with our constituents. Therefore, Madam Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie):
That the matter of the New Democratic Party pamphlet entitled "Our West", printed as a quarterly household mailing by the House of Commons printing office but clearly designed as a party handout of the type normally printed and distributed by the headquarters of a political party, and the disrepute such misuse of publicly-funded facilities is liable to bring to the House of Commons and its members, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to join in echoing the sentiments of my hon. friend from Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight). After examining the so-called householder and looking at the rules clearly established by this House and through the Management and Members' Services Committee, it would seem to me on the surface that the document which my hon. colleague is bringing to the attention of the House is one that constitutes an abuse of the rules. I believe the action that is undertaken by the members of the New Democratic Party is highly improper and it is, indeed, misleading. Because if one looks at pages 18 and 19, one might be led to believe that Saskatchewan has only seven Members of Parliament. I am referring to the seven New Democratic Party Members of Parliament.
I believe that it does constitute a blatant abuse of the rules which have been established by this House and by the committee. This is a service which has been provided to all Members of the House of Commons, as pointed out by the member for Kindersley-Lloydminster, and it is essentially for the purpose of communicating our activities, as members, to our constituents as well as the activities of the House of Commons.
It is generally ruled that anything of a partisan nature is not allowable, and therefore distribution of a document is essentially for the purpose of information rather than for the dissemination of anything which could be construed as politically partisan.
November 10, 1981

It is rather strange that the New Democratic Party, which is usually the first one to cry wolf when the rules and procedures of the House are being stretched or encroached upon, is the first one to take advantage of the situation and wallow in the public trough. This comes from a group which is sanctimonious; but on the first examination of this document it would seem to me that the actions that are being taken by the members of the NDP clearly constitute something less than honesty and could very well be ruled as being deceitful.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
In my view, this clearly constitutes an abuse of the privileges of members of this House and it is clearly a case of using public funds for partisan and narrow party purposes.
When I had the privilege of serving as Minister of Transport in this House a couple of years ago, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) was the first one to draw attention to the fact that there was a suggestion that we were infringing upon the rules of the House as a government party in the appointment of members to conduct a study into grain transportation as well as the matter of prairie branch lines.
At that time the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) admonished the members in our party, notwithstanding the fact that the precedent had been clearly established by previous governments that it was allowable that members of one party could be assigned to conduct specific tasks. It was done, for example, in the case of the Hon. Charles M. Drury when he was selected as constitutional adviser for the development of the constitution for the Northwest Territories. The hon. member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) was assigned a special responsibility by the government for the purpose of assisting the minister in developing the proper framework for negotiations with respect to northern and native land claims.
Notwithstanding that precedent, and notwithstanding the fact that the Speaker at that time ruled that it was not illegal but may be on the verge of being improper, our party acknowledged the admonition of the Speaker and undertook to pay the expenses which were involved as a result of the publication of this document which was commissioned by myself and undertaken by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil).

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
I should say as well, to illustrate the fact that the document was intended to do a job that was clearly necessary to carry out public transportation policies, that after the matter had been clarified and the invoice had been paid and settled by the Progressive Conservative Party, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) asked if we would release the report to him and he would refund any costs that were involved as a result of the printing. I agreed to that and that has been done. The report is now public.
I think it clearly shows that while there may well have been some question about the methodology, the action taken by our
Privilege-Mr. McKnight
party was sincere and was taken in a manner which was deemed to be necessary-that a clear statement of government policy at that time be undertaken.
I believe when you examine this matter, Madam Speaker, you might want to reflect on the exchange which took place at that time. Now the shoe is on the other foot. You may want to remind the members of the New Democratic Party of some of the rhetoric they espoused in the House of Commons when they took exception to the manner in which our work was being carried out.
I should say that the then hon. member for Nickel Belt, who fortunately or unfortunately is not with us at present, had some very harsh things to say about the process undertaken by us when we were in government. At page 2142 of Hansard, for December 7, 1979, he is reported as saying:
The Conservative Party does not need to eat at the public trough to have a study done with a partisan slant.
I think it is quite obvious that while he may have some opinions about who is eating at the public trough, the then Minister of Transport did not see this as a partisan document. Nevertheless, that is behind us. I simply point that out to you, Madam Speaker.
There is an obligation, indeed a responsibility, on all of us to ensure that fairness and justice not only be done but appear to be done. It is equally important for all of us to accept our responsibility in ensuring that we work toward overcoming the cynicism that does prevail and is associated with Members of Parliament, indeed, the institution.
I humbly submit that the actions of the New Democratic Members of Parliament are such that they are not enhancing the calibre and the credibility of this institution but, in fact, are eroding confidence and adding to cynicism. I suggest that they should do what we did when there was a question of doubt. Rather than the public and the House of Commons paying for this highly partisan document, it should be paid for out of New Democratic coffers.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened with interest and, I must confess, with some degree of shock to the statements made by both the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). I find it interesting that when viewing something which was done by his own party the hon. member for Vegreville could find that it was done with sincerity, integrity and honesty, while attributing to another member from another party that what was done by that member was done without those same three ingredients.
To begin with, I want to suggest that the document which has been placed before Your Honour is not a document which was in any way considered to be a political document. It was considered by the hon. member to be within the jurisdiction of his responsibility to inform people in his province of the role being played by members they elected. It was never intend-

November 10, 1981
Privilege-Mr. McKnight
ed-neither is it intended now-to place a slant on any of the roles of any of the other members. Neither did it make reference to that.
I suggest to Your Honour that if you were to undertake a review of the documents sent out under the names of various and many members of this House of Commons under the guise of reports, which we undoubtedly will now begin to do, you would find that there are very few, if any, that do not contain some degree of partisan material. For a member to rise in his place in an attempt to leave the impression that to indicate a degree of partisanship in any of the reports is somehow a departure from the normal practice is, in my judgment, to be quite untruthful.
I want to put to Your Honour something of which I am sure Your Honour is quite aware, that is, that the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) is as honest a man as there is in this House, that his integrity is without question, and that for some Tory in a sleazy way to try to indicate that this hon. member has done something wrong is appalling.
If the hon. members who have risen honestly believe that there is a need for Your Honour to review the document, we have no objection. If in your judgment Your Honour was to find that there has been some minor deviation from accepted norms we will, of course, accept that judgment. But I am confident that Your Honour will see through what is undoubtedly a partisan attempt by certain Conservative members to discredit the hard work of the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, and I ask Your Honour to disregard those submissions and to find that there has been no deviation from accepted practice.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my intervention will be very brief, but it will touch upon a matter which was not raised by the hon. member who suggested that there is a question of privilege here to be considered-and I speak in support of that submission-nor was it touched upon by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) did not touch on anything.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: I got to the root of it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
Once again I want to draw your attention, Madam Speaker, to what I suppose one would call a memo of explanation or a memo of clarification which was sent around by Mr. A. Silverman dated October 7, 1981, part of which has already been quoted by the hon. member who raised this matter. In support of my submission to Your Honour I wish to emphasize the use of the words on page 2 "is to enable members to convey information to their constituents," it is not for the purpose of conveying information to the constituents of other members. Householder mailings are for the purpose of conveying information to a particular member's constituents. That is the narrow stricture placed upon the use of householder mailings. If it were not to be so interpreted, there would be nothing to prevent any member of this House from using his householder privileges to address mailings to the constituents
of any other member or members of the House of Commons. I am sure that that was not the intention when the service was originally set up, and I am certain it would not be the wish of members of this House to impose that kind of added cost to the expense of running this place which, in the final analysis, is paid by the taxpayer.
Having laid that groundwork, may I again refer Your Honour to the introductory page in the offensive pamphlet. In the third paragraph at the second line it says "even though some of you don't live in constituencies represented by a New Democrat". It does not say "even though some of you might not live in a constituency represented by a New Democrat"; it says specifically "even though some of you don't live in constituencies represented by a New Democrat." There is a clear implication there that this political pamphlet has been mailed throughout the province of Saskatchewan to people who do not live in constituencies represented by New Democratic Party members. There can be no doubt, therefore, I submit, that the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) has raised a very valid question of privilege.
The additional point I want to make in support of a reference to committee has to do with a matter on which you, Madam Speaker, and I have exchanged some correspondence, namely, the proper use of members' franking privileges. These pamphlets are not distributed-I do not think this particular one is-by New Democratic members and their workers in the province of Saskatchewan, but I could be wrong there.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: You don't know.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: The clear implication is that they have been mailed from this House of Commons under members' franking privileges. That was never intended.

subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: How do you know that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
I do not know that, but I am asking hon. members and you, Madam Speaker, to draw the very clear inference that that conclusion is inescapable in the absence of any explanation, and there has been none, that mailing privileges of members have been abused as well.
The whole matter could be cleared up, as suggested by the hon. member for Vegreville. Although he did not make the direct suggestion, I do. The whole matter could be cleared up if the House leader of the New Democratic Party as a representative of his party would rise in his place and give the assurance that he is prepared to discharge any costs incurred in the printing and distribution of this political pamphlet.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext: Including the postage.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
Including the postage. In any event, since I do not anticipate that will happen, it seems to me, and it certainly is my strong submission to Your Honour, that there has been a solid case made out that goes beyond the mere requirement that Your Honour reach a conclusion that a prima facie case exists and therefore merits the matter's being sent to committee. There seems to be an inescapable conclusion which leaves
November 10, 1981

no doubt that there has been an abuse. There has been no explanation forthcoming, and therefore I submit that your finding should be that there is a prima facie case and that the matter should be referred to committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. MCKNIGHT-HOUSEHOLDER PRODUCED BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
speechtext:
I think there is one part of this question I can clear up quite readily. Although the mailing of the householders of Members of Parliament is a privilege, I do not believe it falls under the definition of privilege as described in Standing Order 17. I do not feel that this is a question of privilege in the sense that was invoked by the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight). However, it seems it does raise a new aspect of our printing guidelines, which have recently been clarified. Perhaps we will need to clarify them even more after this occurrence.
Since 1 have been in the chair, the management and members' services committee have asked me to modify somewhat the rules and guidelines concerning householders in the sense that they felt it should not be left in the hands of bureaucrats to evaluate or tell Members of Parliament what they may or may not say to their constituents. 1 may say I fully agreed with that; it was putting a responsibility on the bureaucrats that did not belong to them.
Obviously if our printing service printed this particular householder, they looked at what they were printing to see whether there was some flagrant misuse of the privilege. Because they printed this one, they obviously felt it did not contravene the guidelines. Since we have removed that responsibility from the bureaucrats, I will not give it back to them. I will look at this householder against the guidelines set by the committee to see whether they need to be further clarified.
Members should keep in mind that what is partisan to one member is sometimes not partisan to another. It would have to be more than an opinion about a certain issue that was expressed in order for me or anyone else in this House to decide that it was partisan. But perhaps we will have to clarify the guidelines.
I have not completely read the householder in question. As I look at it, I see nothing at first glance that would permit me to say that it is a flagrant abuse of the privileges of Members of Parliament. However, I think it would be wise for me to look at it more carefully against the arguments presented to me in the House today, and perhaps, if I find there is reason for doing so, send a request to the members' services committee in general terms so that they will look at the guidelines and see whether there is a possibility of clarifying them in order to avoid this kind of occurrence or misinterpretation of the guidelines.
It is not always easy to interpret the guidelines. That is why we have removed that from the bureaucrats. I certainly do not want to be in the position of having to read all householders and determine as Speaker whether they are in accordance with the guidelines. We feel very strongly, and I think every member will support me in this position, that members them-
Privilege-Mr. Lewis
selves should take responsibility for what they write in these householders against the guidelines which they have made for themselves.
Basically the responsibility is with the member. The member bears the onus of having bypassed or gone beyond the guidelines, and that is it. He stands or falls on the fact that he is interpreting the use of his own privileges in a way that is considered to be proper. I will look at this question and take it under advisement.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I gave you notice of a question of privilege which arises out of today's question period. Today the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), who is responsible for housing, admitted in this House that officials of his department had advised some home owners to wait until Thursday or Friday of this week to resolve their difficulties. I submit that this is a clear breach of the traditional secrecy which surrounds budgets. There is a very large difference between Thursday and Friday to every Canadian home owner.
We have posed questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in this House. He has quite rightly not answered any questions in the House directly affecting the budget. As a matter of fact, on October 20, 1981, as reported at page 11964 of Hansard, the minister stated:
It is easy enough to ask whether "A" will be in the budget and whether "B" will be in the budget and, by a process of daily questioning, presumably, the budget would be produced by instalments, and then hon. members would be saying, "Well, why have you broken budget secrecy?"
I submit that today the minister responsible for housing admitted to either "A" or "B". If his officials are calling members of the Canadian public, and he has admitted they are, with specific knowledge from the Minister of Finance, that is a breach by the Minister of Finance of budget secrecy. There is a second breach. When the minister responsible for housing directs his officials to make certain comments during phone calls to certain Canadian home owners, that is a breach. The third breach is the actual giving of advice to a Canadian home owner by an official in the minister's office.
Budget leaks are often considered to be something which triggers a large capital gain in the stock market, or something which could be said to be depriving the government of revenue. We are not talking here about a big kill on the stock market. We are talking about the basic right of Canadians to the same knowledge as every other Canadian. It is just as vital to the Canadian who owns a home, has contacted his or her Member of Parliament, has then had their name forwarded to the minister's office and receives a phone call from the minister's official, as it is to every other Canadian home owner. We have here a discrimination against every Canadian home owner who renews a mortgage or buys or sells a home.
We have information which has made us aware of an
individual in Delta, B.C. with a mortgage expiring November

November 10, 1981
Privilege-Mr. Lewis
10, 1981, this very day, bearing interest at 13% per cent. The credit union offered to renew the mortgage at 20% per cent. The individual contacted his Member of Parliament, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen). The member contacted the minister's office and an official in the minister's office then contacted that individual. When I talked to that individual last night, he told me that he was advised to stall his renewal until Friday because something would happen Thursday night which would help him.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext: Order. Can the hon. member tell us whose privilege he is discussing? Is it his own privilege or that of his constituent? Constituents do not enjoy privileges under our Standing Orders in the sense that members of the House do. If the hon. member wants to help the Chair with regard to a finding in the case, he has to restrict himself to what constitutes privilege. Up until now I have heard nothing in his intervention which leads me to believe there is a question of privilege in this case.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
My research on the question of budget secrecy did not spell it out as a matter of the privilege of any one individual member, although I submit in this case we may have that. It is rather a question of the privilege of the House and every member of this House to be entitled to the same information at the same time. First, I submit it is a breach of the privileges of every member of this House. Budget secrecy seems to be handled in a different section in the authorities. Second, it is a breach of the privileges of every member of this House, including the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm), who talked about an individual in his constituency who did not receive a call. It is a breach of our privileges when the government does not release the same information at the same time.
Both sides of the House represent different ridings in this country. We all have Canadian home owners in trouble. If the minister were to play fair and square with this House and with the people of Canada, he should issue a press release as soon as he knows what is in the budget and direct all of the institutions, whether it be trust companies, banks or credit unions, not to renew mortgages until after the budget. He should then come into this House and make the same point to the Canadian nation and to everybody at the same time.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
This is so that the hon. members of the House get the same information as the officials in the minister's office.
The leading authority on the question of budget secrecy, what is called the Dalton case in Britain, is where the chancellor of the Exchequer casually mentioned to a reporter that tobacco taxes would rise prior to the budget announcement that evening. The reporter was privy to information that the House did not receive. As a result of the uproar, the minister was given the opportunity to resign. I am referring to the notes
from the Parliamentary Library that were prepared for the House of Commons by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. The document is entitled "Background Information on Government Secrecy, Financial Measures and Parliamentary Secretaries". I draw your attention, Madam Speaker, to page 2572, it looks like to me-I'll confirm that because I am not really sure what it is.
Budget secrecy, in fact, is considered so confidential that even cabinet colleagues to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) are not made aware of the budget proposals until shortly before its presentation in Parliament, and even then they are often provided with only a general outline.
I submit to you, Madam Speaker, that if the minister of housing directed his officials to make telephone calls telling people not to do anything until Friday morning, in effect he is releasing information which is contained in the budget. It is one thing to utter a bland statement in the House that "everybody in the House should wait and see if we address the concerns of Canadians in dire straits"; but it is another thing for an official in the minister's office to phone somebody, based on information he received from a Member of Parliament, and tell that individual to wait until Friday.
If you were to find a breach of the privileges of this House, Madam Speaker, I would propose the following motion:
That the matter of the possession of budget information by members of the ministerial staff of the Minister of Public Works, the communication of budget information by those staff members to individual members of the public with mortgages due, specifically in telling them that mortgage help would be contained in the November 12 budget, and the violation of the necessary constitutional and parliamentary tradition of budget secrecy, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I submit we have not heard anything today that raises a question of privilege. The hon. member used the phrase "that the minister should be fair and square." If we were to be "fair and square" in this House, I think it has to be pointed out that the hon. members of the Liberal Party for the last few weeks have been subjected to a daily barrage from hon. members of the official opposition, in particular where we have heard ministers invited and encouraged to reveal what is in the budget. Today the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) repeatedly asked if a minister would disclose what would be in the budget. Now we have an hon. member of the opposition complaining about something the minister said that could somehow be interpreted as breaking the rule against disclosing anything that might be in the budget. As a result of this, a question of privilege has arisen. The most blatant, double standard I can conceive of is for hon. members to say "disclose", but then if you were to say anything, they say "shame, shame; terrible, terrible".
I suggest that nothing that the minister has stated, or that his officials have done, that we have been advised of indicates that a breach has occurred. The only thing that seems to have taken place is that people have raised issues with which they are concerned. They have even said, "Well, you have to wait for the answer and see what is in the budget." If some tidbit has been tossed out, what is it? What is the information that
November 10, 1981

has been provided to these people? We have not heard anything about that. We have simply been advised that they have been told to wait. Everyone has been told to wait.
I submit this is a totally spurious point of privilege, Madam Speaker, and just a waste of the time of this House.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
I shall be brief, Madam Speaker. The point that is at issue here has to do with the nature of the representation that was given, with the declared authority of the minister responsible for housing, by one of his officials to at least two individuals of the selective 200 that were telephoned by representatives of the minister responsible for housing.
In one case, a citizen in Delta, British Columbia, was explicity told that he should hold off until Friday. Obviously, that information was conveyed with knowledge by the official to the citizen that the budget would come down on Thursday. The inference drawn was that if the citizen were to hold off until Friday, which was the information authorized by the minister of housing and conveyed by his official, there would be something brought down in the budget that would be available to him.
A citizen of Halton was explicitly promised by an official authorized to impart such information by the minister of housing that there would be, and I quote, "help in the budget for people like you." It was not a suggestion that one should wait. It was a clear commitment that there would be help in the budget for people like the person in Halton that had a problem with his house.
The minister responsible for housing admitted in this House earlier today that he authorized those telephone calls. There can be no doubt at all about that. He has said that and he has accepted responsibility for it. He lamented that he did not call more people. However, he made it clear that he authorized those telephone calls. The telephone call he authorized in at least one case told a Canadian citizen explicitly that there would be help in the budget.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext: How do you know that?

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext: That clearly indicated that there was the communication of the nature of a budgetary provision that was not known to the rest of the people of Canada and not known to the House of Commons, but which was conveyed by an official of the minister's office, with the minister's authority.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext: Pure inference.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
That clearly breaches all of the practices in relation to budget secrecy that we have known in this House.
What makes it even more of an affront to hon. members of this House is that, as the hon. member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith) has just indicated, we have been asking time after time in this House, in light of the grave circumstances that Canadians face in the prospect of losing their homes, that if there were to be provisions in the budget with regard to aid for
Privilege-Mr. Lewis
home owners, the exception be clearly made, as a result of all party agreement, to make an early announcement of such. That request has been denied frequently on the floor of the House. What they have refused to do by agreement, they have now done in breach of all budgetary practices.
We have here two instances. One, we have the selective release of information to particular individuals, in the face of a refusal to make a general statement of the nature of that budgetary provision; and second, on the authority of the minister responsible for housing, we have an official telephoning an individual Canadian whom he knew to be interested- not someone chosen at random, but someone whom he knew would benefit from the information-and conveying to that individual the explicit information that there would be help in the budget for people like that individual. When the minister authorized that call to be made, he authorized a call to be made by an official to a person whom he knew would benefit and would have an interest. I believe that falls clearly within the boundary of what has been described in the past as a breach of the privileges of the House and a breach in relation to budget secrecy.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext: The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition; excuse my breach of decorum. I believe there are only two points which we have to make on this. First, for many months now it has been a declared policy of the government to help people who find themselves in dire straits. My second point is also very simple. Anyone who finds himself in dire straits should, if acting prudently, wait until the budget comes down. That is all I have to say on the point.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY

Madam Speaker, sometimes when I intervene on a question of privilege my remarks are somewhat lengthy. I will make my comments very brief today. I had hoped to raise my own question of privilege tomorrow as a result of question period today.
In response to what has just been said, I think it was a rather critical, serious statement that people in dire straits should wait until budget time. The hon. member is disagreeing very definitely with the minister responsible for housing, who repeatedly told the House that there was no need to wait for the budget. He told people to contact their Members of Parliament who will bring their messages directly to the minister responsible, not after budget, not at budget time, but immediately. The exact date of the communication from the minister directly to every Conservative Member of Parliament was October 23.

November 10, 1981
Privilege-Mr. Lewis
I raise a question of privilege which relates directly to each Member of Parliament, particularly Conservative members because they were the ones who received the memo from the minister asking them to act. In all good faith a number of us had the opportunity to return to our ridings to interview people who were in dire straits. It was not because we wanted to leave the House to return to our constituencies, but because the minister responsible for housing asked us if we would in a memo to our offices on October 23. Being interested in the people in dire straits I, as many other Conservative members, returned to my riding; I spent two days there. If this is not a question of privilege I do not know what is.
I took down 32 specific case histories at the request of the minister. My privilege in serving my constituents is seriously affected by this very issue. After two days I brought the case histories back to the House with all the mortgage information I was requested to obtain. I presented them to Madam Speaker in the form of a petition. At the same time, as recorded in Hansard on November 2, I delivered them across the House to the minister responsible because he had specifically requested them.
What has happened since that date is the basis of my question of privilege. My constituents have never heard one word, not a peep, not a telephone call, not a letter, not a communique, not a wire, not an indirect message through a mortgage company back to them, as a result of what appears to be the minister wasting the time of Members of Parliament when they could be better serving their constituents.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY

Order, please. If that is what constitutes a question of privilege in the hon. member's mind, I must interrupt him to say that the manner in which a minister responds to a petition or to a request of any kind from a Member of Parliament may constitute a grievance of great importance in the hon. member's mind-and I do not deny that-but certainly it is not a question of privilege.
If the hon. member has a new argument relating to this question I can hear it, but I cannot allow him at this point, because I have heard enough speakers, to debate the question of hon. members not being satisfied that the minister has properly answered petitions, letters or requests or that some have received answers and others have not. This is not a matter which the Chair can determine. It might be a grievance on the part of a member, but that is all it is; it is not a question of privilege.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, It is my understanding that a valid question of privilege is a question as to whether the law of contempt of Parliament has been breached. Therefore, I should like to put to you whether you judge it proper that a motion be put to the House on the matter I should now like to describe.
The minister of the government responsible for CMHC is well documented in Hansard and elsewhere as desiring that his fellow members forward information to him. I hasten to add that I am raising this matter with Madam Speaker on behalf of all hon. members of the House who have constituents in this
deplorable situation. I now find that the minister's parliamentary staff has informed certain home owners by telephone of information which by every right, rule and precedent of the House should be the exclusive prerogative of the House. I am referring to the information contained in the much-delayed budget which the House can hopefully expect to come down on Thursday.
The reasons for confidentiality of the budget before it is brought down are well known and require little elaboration. It seems to me to be an equally valid point that the effect of the budget must be exerted and felt in a completely uniform manner throughout all sectors of the economy and society. If budget information is being prematurely passed on to certain individuals by the minister, information which Parliament must necessarily be advised of in the first instance by means of the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen), then the law of contempt of Parliament should clearly be cited and my rights as an individual member are surely being circumvented.
In view of there appearing to be sufficient cause to establish a prima facie case of breach of privilege, and in so far as it appears that privilege is sufficiently involved that it should take precedence over House business, I should like to support the motion that this matter be referred for full investigation into whether certain constituents in Canada have been privileged to receive certain information. I know for a fact that not one of the 32 people in the Peterborough area have ever received a telephone call. They were not aware until today that there was to be something in the budget at 8 p.m. this Thursday.

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY

speechtext:
Order, please. I think I heard a sufficient number of interventions on the particular point. It is quite puzzling to me that most of the facts brought forward in the question of privilege seem to be of a hypothetical nature. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) said in his summation that if the minister in fact instructed his officials to say a certain thing to constituents then he would feel, etc. This is hypothetical; no one knows whether the minister did. Even if a minister said a certain thing to a constituent, I do not feel that that in itself represents a question of privilege. I might add that we do not know for a fact whether the constituents reported exactly how the conversation with the official occurred. That too is somewhat hypothetical in the way it is presented to the House. Thus it makes it very difficult for me to say there is anything other than grievances on the part of hon. members who are complaining about the conduct of the minister or of officials of the minister. There is no question of privilege.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said it is quite clear that the minister authorized the calls. I think the hon. minister has acknowledged in the House that he has
November 10, 1981

authorized officials of his department to call a number of constituents concerning their difficulties with their mortgages. In this particular matter I do not see any question of privilege either.
At any rate, we do not know if the minister did dictate the answer which the officials gave to those constituents. Even if he had, I think the minister is free to deal with these complaints in the manner which he chooses. Certainly the Chair cannot determine how the minister will deal with them. Unfortunately again, it might constitute a grievance on the part of hon. members on the other side of the House, but it certainly is not a question of privilege.
The other question which is being argued is that there has been a leak of the budgetary measures to come. We do not really know because we do not know what those measures are; but certain sentences pronounced by the minister are interpreted as being a leak or as giving advance knowledge to certain selective persons of what is contained in the budget.
I will not pass judgment on whether it is or is not a leak, or whether the words chosen were wise or cautious. 1 just want to remind hon. members that the matter of budget secrecy is a convention and is not a matter for the Chair to enforce. It is a convention. It is true that in Great Britain a certain minister resigned because he had-

Another very real difficulty that Your Honour-

subtopic: MR. LEWIS-ALLEGED BREACH BY MINISTER OF BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
I have two matters to raise which are different and which flow from Your Honour's very careful comments. The first relates to the underlining of the fact, with which certainly all of us in the House agree, that convention clearly establishes that if there has been a breach of budget secrecy, the practice, as established by Mr. Dalton in Great Britain, is that the minister who broke the budget secrecy should resign. That, I think, is worth having on the record.
The other matter I think Your Honour may have suggested inadvertently, and which I would not want to rest on the record of the House, was that despite the authorization of the minister to make calls, if in fact those calls were made, the nature of those calls and any breach of budgetary secrecy which may flow from those calls would be the responsibility of the public servant involved and not that of the minister.
I am sure that was not what Your Honour intended to suggest, but I think that your remarks, on rereading them, may be open to that interpretation. Certainly I wanted to rise at the earliest possible opportunity to again underline the view which has been long held by those of us in this party, that when an official acts on the instruction of a minister, then the minister is responsible, by our system, for the actions of that official, and that that responsibility cannot be passed off to the official.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order resulting from yesterday's question period, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) once again referred to women members in the House as "honourable lady" and "lady", and made other disparaging remarks, while consistently referring to male members-

subsubtopic: MRS. MITCHELL-USE OF EXPRESSION "HONOURABLE LADY"
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MRS. MITCHELL-USE OF EXPRESSION "HONOURABLE LADY"
speechtext: -as "honourable members".

subsubtopic: MRS. MITCHELL-USE OF EXPRESSION "HONOURABLE LADY"
speechtext: You are not a lady, eh?

subsubtopic: MRS. MITCHELL-USE OF EXPRESSION "HONOURABLE LADY"
speechtext:
I am sure I represent the concerns of other hon. members in the House. Some hon. members in the House find this attitude offensive and inequitable.
The Oxford Dictionary defines "lady" as "ruling woman; woman to whom man is chivalrously devoted; mistress; woman belonging to the upper class". While the first term, "ruling woman" may refer to Your Honour, I think that the others are probably inappropriate.
Therefore, in light of modern times, and in view of the outdated and sexist overtones of both the terms "honourable lady" or "honourable gentleman", I want to ask Your Honour if you will declare these terms to be obsolete or unparliamentary and require that all members, regardless of sex, be referred to with equal respect as "honourable members".

subsubtopic: MRS. MITCHELL-USE OF EXPRESSION "HONOURABLE LADY"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MRS. MITCHELL-USE OF EXPRESSION "HONOURABLE LADY"
speechtext: Let the record show that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) approves.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MRS. MITCHELL-USE OF EXPRESSION "HONOURABLE LADY"
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) for raising this problem. However, I think that she is probably referring to a circumstance in the House when I did rise in order to ask an hon. member not to address, between brackets, a member of the feminine sex as the "lady member". That is quite different from the "honourable lady" or the "honourable gentleman".
In my view, I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did use an acceptable expression when he said the "honourable lady". He did say, "If I can say the honourable gentleman, it follows that I may say the honourable lady".
What I did not accept in the House, and I think the hon. member will recall the circumstances, was a member referring to a member of feminine sex as the lady member. I think that would be offensive because there are no lady members and no men members; they are simply members of this House.
I may add that in other parliaments certain expressions are accepted. For instance, "my hon. friend". If a member is referring to a Member of Parliament who sits on the same side of the House, he is called an hon. friend. If the member sits on the other side of the House, he is called the hon. gentleman. The expression "hon. friend" is limited, 1 understand, to those who sit on the same side of the House. Those are other practices.
I think we can accept the practice in this House of referring to members of the feminine sex as hon. ladies. That is not offensive, any more than it is offensive to refer to members of the masculine sex as hon. gentlemen.
