The House resumed, from Monday, November 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-48, to regulate oil and gas interests in Canada lands and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, be read the third time and do pass.
Canada Oil and Gas Act

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been looking forward to speaking on third reading for some time. We have spent much time on this bill. Some of that time was usefully employed, although major changes were not made and the bill has in many ways been tidied up.
Before I get into a discussion of the principles of this bill, principles that we still find objectionable, I would like to correct the record, so to speak. In the presentation made last night by the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), he said that when the matter was before the committee the suggestion was made that the committee travel to those provinces and the northern territories most affected by the bill. He said that move had been objected to by members of this party.
That is not correct and he knows that full well. I believe he would appreciate the record being straightened out. The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap is not so badly imbued with the rhetoric of his party that he is beyond redemption, like some other members, for instance the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), and I am sure he will see the error of his ways.
I have a few words about the process we have been going through for nearly a year concerning this bill. We first might object to the fact that there was no real consultation in the drafting of this bill with the governments and the provinces affected or with the governments of the territories affected. If we look at the history of the development of northern oil and gas legislation, we will see that in past times, for instance when Bill C-20 was before this House some years ago, there was a good deal of consultation with industry, with other governments at other levels and with people who would be affected generally. This was not the case when Bill C-48 was introduced. The government decided unilaterally what it wanted to do and it did not want to be dissuaded from any of its erroneous ideas by getting advice of other affected persons at the beginning.
I cannot fault the government on the time it has allowed for debate on this bill. In fact, the government has been more generous than usual. I rather suspect that is because the government has nothing else it would like to put before Parliament at this time and is just using this bill as a filler until the government eventually brings in its budget, and the Constitution, if it ever gets around to that.
Although we cannot fault the government on the amount of time allowed, we certainly can fault it for the fact that it has not been able to see fit to change its ideas in the least. I have the impression that what we have been doing for many months now is just beating our heads against a brick wall, because it has not budged one little bit.
The principles contained in the bill are exactly the same ones in the bill one year ago. It would be my supposition that the spirit of Parliament has been violated. Usually when new legislation comes before this House there is a process of give and take and compromise, but in this instance with Bill C-48 that parliamentary spirit of compromise has just not worked.

November 10, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Bill C-48 is one of the most radical proposals brought before this House for many years. It is radical in many ways, but the government, egged on by its colleagues in the NDP, has imposed a very socialist framework on probably what in years to come will be the most important segment of the Canadian oil and gas industry. The government has certainly made no bones about the fact that this is the direction in which it wishes to proceed, the direction of state control over oil and gas in northern Canada and in those offshore areas in the maritime provinces.
We look at the objectionable principles contained in the bill and see that in regard to every piece of land on which oil and gas exploration and production will take place it is the government's desire to have government participation. There is not only the question of having a federal Crown corporation acting in normal competition with the private sector; what the government wants is government involvement in every little parcel of land. It does not want anyone to be free of having the state as a partner.
We see contained in the bill the concept of retroactive expropriation. Governments at the municipal, provincial and federal levels must have the power of expropriation. There are times, unfortunately, when this power has to be used. The example that most often comes to mind is the construction of the St. Lawrence Seaway. Lands owned by individuals along the route of the seaway, because of national overriding interests, had to be taken away from those owners. In that circumstance proper compensation was generally paid.
What will be done through this bill is expropriation of something that has already been granted and is not needed because of an overriding national concern. There is no great need for the government to rush in and take away 25 per cent of the land holdings of companies. If the government wanted, it could apply this principle of a Crown reserve to new dispositions of oil and gas rights. But to go in and retroactively expropriate that which has been previously given to someone, without even proper compensation, is surely something we in this House as Canadians should not accept. If expropriation is to take place, surely one of the principles that we should hold dear is that proper compensation be given. We supported this principle in various motions put before the House at report stage. That is not to be the case with Bill C-48.
The government or the state will take over 25 per cent of an undertaking and then repay part of the moneys previously spent on exploration and development out of future production. What kind of a deal is that, I ask, Mr. Speaker? I submit that if we proceed with legislation like this citizens and corporations which operate in Canada will never again be able to take the government of the day at its word.
Years ago there were generous provisions for the disposition of oil and gas rights because that was deemed by the government of the day to be necessary. The government had to give people a fairly easy deal to get them into the country to spend the money and the time. A few years later when exploration results are reasonably successful, in comes the same government and says: "We have changed the rules of the game now.
Sure, we said that to suck you in and get you to spend your money, but now that you have been successful and have found something worth having, we are going to take that away from you." What could be more improper?
Another principle of this bill relates to the way in which dispositions are to be made-the company to government deals that will have to be made. Previously, and as far as I know this has occurred in most provincial jurisdictions to date, oil and gas rights were disposed of in one of two ways, either on a first come, first served basis, or by public tender.
In the old days in the Northwest Territories, if you wanted to acquire an oil and gas lease you went in and physically marked out the boundaries of the area you wanted by blazing trees and putting in corner posts, very much in the same way as you would stake out a mineral claim. If you were the first person to go into an area and do that, you acquired title to that particular lease.
A little later on it was deemed unnecessary to go in and physically mark out the area. The country was divided into a series of areas or units along lines of latitude and longitude. The first person or corporation applying for one of these areas, providing the necessary fee was paid and an undertaking was given to do the necessary work, would receive the rights to that piece of land, on a first come, first served basis.
Another way of disposing of oil and gas rights is by public tender. If the owner of the oil and gas rights, the government, decides to dispose of a particular parcel of land, it is put up for disposal and every party is able to tender, either in terms of an amount of cash payable to the government or on a work commitment-the amount of work the interested party will do on that piece of land-and the one who makes the best offer publicly is the one to whom the oil and gas rights are given.
In the bill before us those two fair and equitable systems have been thrown out. If someone wants oil and gas rights, they have to see the minister or someone who works for him. They have to work out their own deal and it does not go to the person who gets there first. It does not necessarily go to the person who offers the best deal, nor is it publicly determined. It goes to the one who is the smoothest talker, perhaps. It may go to the one for whom the minister wants to do a special favour. I suggest there are many dangers involved-patronage and all the other things we associate with the banana republics. That is what will occur with this type of legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
If we examine the nature of the dispositions to be made, we find that the time-honoured Canadian concept of the oil and gas lease is no longer there. The nature of ownership will be something much less than fee-simple ownership or lease-type ownership at the exploration stage. In the past a company had an exploration permit in the north. Under this legislation it will have to enter into some form of exploration agreement, as the government calls it. Such an agreement will not give any title at all to that oil and gas or to the land.
November 10, 1981

An agreement under this legislation will only allow a company to do a limited amount of work on a specified piece of land. The exclusivity and degree of title is no longer there.
Even if this argument were valid in the case of exploration, in my opinion this approach should not be adopted when it comes to production. Instead of the 21-year lease or the 10-year lease for the purpose of production, such as was given out in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia and other places, the highest form of tenure available under the measure before us will be the so-called production licence. This licence is something similar to a driver's licence or a licence to brew home made beer. It will not give title to the land or the oil and gas thereunder.
We have seen in Bill C-48 a concept of preventing people from having proper tenure to a holding. The intent of the bill is to have explorers and producers of oil and gas act as some form of contractor for the government. In a country such as ours where property rights have always been dear to us, I think this is a step in the wrong direction. However, it is a step we see taking place because of the action of members on the other side and to my left. We are seeing the erosion of property rights, whether it be the right to the lot on which we have our house or the right to own oil and gas somewhere in this country. That is why property rights were taken out of the proposed Constitution. We on this side of the House have stated that property rights must be incorporated in the Constitution and should be incorporated in legislation such as Bill C-48.
Another principle in the bill is the concept of strict control by the government over every aspect of the oil and gas industry. The ministerial discretion provided for under this bill allows the minister to tell a company where it can explore, how it can explore, with whom it can explore, and if the minister is not satisfied he can say that Petro-Canada will do the exploration on the company's behalf and take over the management of that piece of land. The company will still be obliged to pay Petro-Canada for what is done even though it may not necessarily be what the company wishes. Under the provisions of this bill the minister can tell a company where to drill, how deep, and the manner in which the well is to be drilled. It will dictate all the technical terms under which the drilling is to be carried out. I believe the government has a mandate to ensure that wells are drilled in a safe manner and that oil is produced in accordance with good conservation procedures. But the government should not go beyond that.
Where does private enterprise and initiative fit into this bill? I suggest this measure provides for state control through the back door. This legislation is pretence. We are pretending we still have a free and independent oil and gas industry in Canada, but if hon. members opposite get their way this will not be the case because the industry will be under the control of the government. That is what they are working toward.
The manner in which the government will control profits and cash flow is objectionable to me. Not only does Bill C-48 provide for this, but it is contained in the National Energy Program under the provisions of the petroleum incentives
Canada Oil and Gas Act
program. The government does not want to conduct the affairs of the Canadian oil and gas industry in the old way, in which people would invest money in oil exploration and if they were lucky enough to find oil and gas in areas accessible to markets they would make a profit. I believe the industry should still be conducted in that way. As profits mount the better it is, since it provides incentive for people to invest further. However, the government does not view it this way. It wants to impose a very high level of taxation on the production of oil and gas.
The so-called progressive incremental royalty system virtually guarantees that a company will not make a greater return on investment in oil and gas than it would on a controlled utility. It maximizes the rate of return on an investment to a minimum. Therefore, the profit incentive will not be there for the investor.
The government wants to take a huge revenue, channel some of it back again through the petroleum incentives program and then decide which company will be eligible for the grant. The government is discarding the traditional way in which we have always proceeded with our business affairs in this country and is replacing it with strict control of the industry. It controls it from the initial investment through to the ultimate profits. That is the basic plan behind Bill C-48.
I believe the real reason why these measures are being put into place was given by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in a speech he made recently in Sherbrooke. It is a speech which was reported to this House by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone).
There seems to be the idea that the hinterland of Canada, which is any place outside the Montreal or Toronto areas, exists for the benefit of that central area. I am not really talking about this in geographical terms, but I am trying to picture a big Liberal cesspool some place which is just sucking in moneys from all over the rest of Canada. The idea is that no place outside this central area gets too powerful or has any real say; control is to be exercised by the government here in Ottawa, and those other areas in the country have to be content with being told what to do, what investments are to be made in the areas and what little profits can remain there, and everything else comes back to Ottawa. There is a very centralized and bureaucratic control over certain parts of Canada from which the Liberal government does not draw many of its supporters.
Now I would like to make a few comments about the Canada lands. We have talked about this subject at some length, and there have been many objections from this side of the House about the use of the term "Canada lands." My colleague the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) has spoken on several occasions in this House about the rights of the Atlantic provinces. The hon. member has dwelt at great length on the historical and legal claims those provinces have to the areas off their shores. I think all of us know that this matter will eventually be decided in the courts, and it might be a little premature for the Government of Canada to assume

November 10, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
what the results of those findings at law will be. I suspect that at least some of the views put forward by the Atlantic provinces will be upheld by the Canadian courts.
With respect to the Atlantic provinces, the government at least made an offer to share revenues. I suppose the reason it did this was so that the matter would not be pursued at law. The government at least made an offer to share revenues derived from the exploitation or possible exploitation of oil and gas in those areas with the provinces concerned.
However, the balance of the Canada lands is basically the territorial lands of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. As limited as the government was in its generosity to Atlantic Canada, it is prepared to extend absolutely nothing to the territories. This is an indecent grab from a defenceless people. If the Atlantic provinces did not have the law on their side, I am sure they would be treated in a manner similar to the disgusting manner in which the people of the two northern territories have been treated.
I listened with interest to the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Kelly) when he spoke about Bill C-48. I am going to cut out his speech and use it during my next election campaign. He gave a very lucid explanation of the view of the Liberal party as to what should happen in the Canadian north. He was very proud of the fact that the policy of the people on his side of the House is to exploit and control the territories. In no way does he ever see responsible government in those territories. In no way does he ever see the attainment of provincial status and the ownership of resources, which is the one thing that binds every other Canadian province together. He was quite frank when he stated that the oil, gas and mineral resources of the north, the agricultural land and everything else should, in perpetuity, belong to the federal government. That is something I would never accept, and I do not think anyone else living in the northern territories of Canada could bring himself to accept it either.
In an earlier presentation to the House with respect to one of the motions we moved, I brought the attention of the House to the fact that if things go the way they possibly might, as bad as the colonial system of government in the north is right now, we might end up with an even worse system. In such a worse system the government of the north would not be conducted by bureaucracy and by government department as it is at present, but would be conducted by Petro-Canada, a commercial Crown corporation-

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Multinationals, maybe?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
-and that, in my opinion, would be the most detrimental thing that could happen. I make the analogy of the government of Rupert's Land, which was conducted by the Hudson's Bay Company, or the government of what is now known as Indonesia, which was conducted by the Dutch East India Company. That is the type of thing into which we could get ourselves.
The hon. lady to my left asks about multinationals. I have dealt with that before. In the case of Petro-Canada the Crown
is there as a regulator and as an operator at the same time and cannot properly undertake its regulatory function. However, in the case of a large multinational oil company the government can exercise its function of a regulator in a proper manner because such corporations are subject to laws of general application. In the case of Petro-Canada, we have already seen that the laws can be changed at will by the government. The government has justified this by saying that Petro-Canada does not have to obey the normal laws of the country because that is the government's chosen instrument; that it is acting in the best interests of the nation; and that therefore we can forget the rights of the people who live in the area concerned, and Petro-Canada can bulldoze right over them.
It is the view of hon. members in my party that the territories should develop economically and constitutionally. In the not too distant future we see the creation of provinces in the north. We see those provinces joining the Canadian confederation. I hope I am around to see that achievement. I hope I am around when the thousands of people who live in the north under the colonial jurisdiction of the Ministry of Indian Affairs and Northern Development eventually join Canada in confederation and are the same as any other citizens of this great country. If that is to happen, the governments of those new provinces must have access to proper revenues with which to conduct government. If the oil, gas and mineral resources are alienated in the way suggested by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board, there will never be a proper government in that area.
My colleagues on this side of the House have described how for many years the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan had to fight to get access to resources in order to provide all the conveniences and necessities of government in that area, and we look forward to the same thing for the territories. We do not look forward to being tied to federal purse strings but to having sufficient revenues to conduct the affairs of autonomous government. That is not to say that we would not be prepared to share with the rest of Canada. We suggest that the federal authorities there retain reasonable powers of taxation to derive from those areas revenues sufficient for their purposes, but we do not want the resources and revenues of the north used to fill the Liberal cesspool to which I referred earlier.
I referred on previous occasions to the trust nature of ownership of resources in the north. It is the considered opinion of myself and those on this side of the House that the land of the territories is held in trust for the eventual provinces to be established there and for the people who will reside in those areas.
I do not want to pursue the arguments over and over; we have made them on several occasions. However, I would like to quote from an editorial in the Yukon News of October 28, 1981 headlined "Yukoners blind to resource robbery". I do not think they are blind to what is going on. The Yukoners I
November 10, 1981

talked to know full well the intentions of the Liberal government. I quote:
This existing situation represents a trust... we have placed in the hands of the federal government the Yukon's dowry of the future.
In olden times, a threat against a daughter's dowry was inexcusable, the dowry protected at all costs because it was the only way a daughter could make a "good" marriage.
So should Yukoners be standing up to protect their dowry, their assurement of entry into the brotherhood of the provinces.
That is the gist of what we have said on many occasions. If these areas of Canada are to come into confederation and have their rightful role in the future of Canada, they cannot have stripped from them now by way of Bill C-48 those things which will enable them to become full provinces.
The other day the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) suggested that what the government was doing was grabbing everything it could right now, and then if at some future time it was forced into the position of having to grant provincial status, it would be handing out to the governments of the new provinces at that time a sucked out lemon. That is the way the hon. gentleman put it and I suggest to you the analogy is to be respected.
By way of Bill C-48 and other legislation and policies put forward by this government, I suggest that in the north they are sewing the seeds of bitterness. I hope that it will not be a tearful harvest. If they are not prepared at this time to at least vest within the territories some degree of ownership over their own resources, they should be prepared to enter into a revenuesharing agreement of the nature proposed for the offshore provinces. There is absolutely no reason why that should not be done.
I suspect there is a propensity on the part of all Members of Parliament, with the possible exception of the cabinet, that something along these lines should be done. Revenue-sharing is quite reasonable and attainable. We can work out some form of compromise on a formula to be used.
Although the government is not prepared to write the provisions of a revenue-sharing agreement within Bill C-48, I urge that it use some other mechanism whereby this can be done and a certain amount of discretionary income can be granted to the northern territories so they do not have to come back time after time, hat in hand, to the federal treasury in Ottawa. When they do that and have their budget carried within the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, it puts them continuously under the thumb of that department. There is a situation whereby duly elected members are not able to carry out the wishes of the constituents but rather are obliged to follow financial and other dictates of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro).
I see you signalling to me, Mr. Speaker. According to my estimate, I have 20 minutes left. Is that correct?

I know the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) has a lot of words of wisdom we should listen to. Therefore, I will not give members the benefits of the two or three pages of advice I have here. I do not know how much of that advice would prove useful to hon. members opposite. I am sure they would find it rather interesting. With Your Honour's indulgence, I will just sum up what will be the likely effects of this bill.
There are some minor good points in the bill. At least the industry will know where it stands. There is likely to be a bit more activity on the so-called Canada lands than at present. However, I do not think there will be anywhere near the amount of activity there would have been had the government laid down proper guidelines and legislation which would have encouraged development by investor-owned corporations and the initiative of people in the oil and gas industry. It has slowed down our goal of self-sufficiency. This slowing down process seems to be quite prevalent on the opposite side. You only have to look at the Norman Wells oil field expansion.
We have the utility concept of the oil and gas business in Canada. We have the idea that the oil and gas industry should have its rate of return controlled and that that industry will be controlled, or within that industry the major say will be had by the Crown corporation, Petro-Canada, in conjunction with certain other large organizations. The large, integrated oil companies that the NDP pretend to dislike so much will be the people running and principally engaged in the Canadian oil and gas business. The little guys will be out. Most are just about out now. They cannot put up with this situation.
Canadians in this business are largely having to look offshore. They are looking towajd the United States. They have been driven out by actions of the Liberal government, supported by their friends, the NDP. They can get a much better deal in other jurisdictions.
In my opinion, with this bill we are sacrificing self-sufficiency or the rapid attainment thereof, Canadian enterprise, the energy future of Canada and the real future of the Canadian north. This is being done on the altar of left-wing idealism and bureaucratic aggrandizement.

They are gravely concerned that this bill will have a detrimental effect on those two items. They also maintain that this bill makes a mockery of land claim negotiations. 1 think some of those concerns have been expressed by my colleagues. They are really concerned that it gives the minister immense powers, to use their words, and it confirms the colonial status of the north. They go on further to say that it stops the progress of responsible government. I have no doubt about that at all. It contravenes the charter of rights, whatever that charter will be when it is returned to the House. They are still concerned that it does contravene many things in what was supposed to be our charter of rights. We will have to wait and see what is in it when it returns. Fortunately at third reading, and as probably one of the last persons to speak on the bill, I am a little reticent to admit that it will be withdrawn, but I should like to point out some of the concerns from central Canada and specifically from the Peterborough area.
It is my sincere conviction that this Liberal government is attempting to put into place the means to create what I consider a socialist republic here in Canada. It intends to impose this plan of converting this nation into a socialist republic through its budget, in concert with its national energy policy and its Constitution. I know this is bothering some hon. members opposite. It is transferring exploration and recovery incentives to Canada lands. This includes offshore regions. It brings in more revenue from oil and gas that will accrue primarily to the federal government.
It is reducing, without any question at all and they cannot refute this on the other side of the House-the share of the oil companies by 12 per cent, companies that are already leaving for the U.S. and other parts of the world, either by choice or by force. This is in the Liberal government's interest because it will increase their direct share of the oil industry in Canada. Indeed, through this program they are to decrease incentives and subsidies to those companies that have minority Canadian ownership interest, which will lower their market value and thus make a takeover bid by the federal government easier in
the future through the Canadian ownership account. At the same time, the Liberal government seeks to increase the proportion of oil and gas revenue from the provinces.
As nationalization of the oil companies located in Alberta, for example, increases, the provincial revenues decrease because federal oil companies do not have to pay provincial royalties, no matter where they are located. Consequently, the federal Liberal government is determined, in concert with their partners to the left in the House, to nationalize the Canadian oil industry by 1990 and put it in public ownership. The estimated cost to purchase just one firm will be approximately $10.5 million. This cost will be borne directly by the people through the Canadian ownership account.
The government seeks to perpetuate an irrevocable shift in the relationship between the two levels of government in Canada. It seeks to take advantage of the westward economic and demographic trends in this country in two ways: first, by removing the initiatives and awards of such shifts from the western centres to the benefit of the central government; and by disowning the promise of a new federation made to the province of Quebec and to the rest of the country. That promise did not include the moulding of a socialist republic with a strong central government.
This is not the true destiny of Canada, despite the socialist conversion we have undergone under successive Liberal governments which have imposed socialist programs upon the people and have had the people pay for them without having the courage to call them such in an election campaign, namely, the 1980 election.
What is happening here, Mr. Speaker, is that the unholy Liberal triumverate in charge of finance, energy and the Constitution is attempting to snatch power, financial power and constitutional power, from its traditional seat in the provincial legislatures. It will seek to do this at the expense of the unity of our country.
For what, Mr. Speaker? For a grand design born in the precocious and presumptuous mind of one man, and one man only, aided by his loyal and partisan engineers. He is determined to alter the basic, fundamental and historic association of this country, of this constitutional federation, of this democratic union of co-operative levels of government.
If the government was sincere in its stated aims in its energy program, it would not proceed in such a suspect, meddlesome and interfering manner. For one thing, it would not tie itself to the anomalous position of seeking to acquire industrial oil interests in Canada, at the same time seeking to reduce our dependence on oil through conservation. It would not pass on to the consumer the burden of its massive and hypocritical subsidization program to lower the cost of imported oil through the petroleum compensation charge. It would not force the people of Canada to buy foreign-owned oil companies to the detriment of the national deficit and the alienation of foreign resource capital.
The government would have made self-sufficiency in energy a true and legitimate national goal and would have eased the
November 10, 1981

means to that end, rather than using this laudable aim as a cover for power grabbing and a platform for this government to acquire the resource control it needs to blueprint its disastrous vision for a socialist future for Canada.
The government is charting a dangerous direction in its present course. The people of Canada must realize this is a punitive exercise, not only upon them through their tax dollars, but against their futures. We may be witnessing here, Mr. Speaker, not only the perpetration of irrevocable damage to our oil industry-for it is our oil industry one way or the other-but we may also become horrified observers as Canadians to the destruction of our dearly held and highly valued constitutional system, our economic freedom, and our liberty to pursue prosperity through personal determination and not through the high-handed interference of a godlike central government. Like Hansel and Gretel, the Canadian taxpayer has been led into the woods by this government, and they will find out that it is they who are to be cooked, not the "goose" of the oil companies and other corporate interests.
Let me address Bill C-48 before us tonight on third reading, a bill to regulate oil and gas interests on all federal Crown lands and all of the offshore regions, as a member who represents some 90,000 people in the urban-rural area of Peterborough, Ontario. What will Bill C-48 and the other ramifications of the Liberal National Energy Program mean to the people in Peterborough, as it might mean to other people across Canada?
In the first place, it will mean that everyone who uses gasoline, whether to drive to work, to keep machinery running, manufacturers who run generators, elderly citizens who drive to the shops, will be paying, come January, $1.90 for a gallon of gasoline and perhaps $38 to fill the gas tanks of their cars. In Janurary, 1983, just over a year from now, they will be paying $2.40 per gallon, or $48 to fill the gas tanks of their cars. By January 1985, they will be paying $3.10 per gallon of gasoline and they will have to shell out something over $60 to fill the gasoline tanks of their cars.
This is in contrast to a government campaign to hold the price of gasoline in Canada down lower than 18 cents. It is shameful. Is this what Ontarians thought would happen when the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) announced his plan a year ago, along with the dismal $14 billion national annual deficit? Is this what they thought would transpire when the former government was brought down on the 18-cent per gallon increase? I do not think so. As painful and difficult as these increases will be to bear-and I know of no constituent of mine who will easily absorb this amount of increase-it is by no means the only significant and deleterious aspect of this bill and other parts of the National Energy Program.
In the first place, a bill such as this which essentially controls the nature, extent and conditions of oil and gas exploration and development in the remaining tracts of undeveloped land in Canada, must be seen in relation to Canada's energy package as a whole. Petro-Canada is an
Canada Oil and Gas Act
essential and some would say crucial part of the plan. Now some would say that it is a good thing Canada through its federal government is now directly involved in the high stakes energy industry. Some would say that finally Canada is doing something about this foreign ownership about which every Canadian child learns in school. But at what cost?
John Kenneth Galbraith said that it is "the imperatives of technology" and not "the images of ideology" which govern the shape and direction of our larger economic society. However, in the case of Canada's energy sector this does not seem to be true. The primary imperative in Canada must surely be-and I see little evidence anywhere of disagreement on this-the development of our energy resources so as eventually to achieve self-sufficiency in 10 or 15 years. That is agreed by all members of the House-self-sufficiency within a reasonable length of time. Our treasury cannot stand for long the immense drain of our financial resources or, rather, the financial resources of our taxpayers which go to pay for steadily increasing amounts of foreign oil that we find it necessary to import. Foreign oil now costs close to $50 per barrel, and we need 100,000 barrels per day. It is like asking for $50 from every man, woman and child in my riding just to pay for the imported oil for one day.
It is clear that we must reduce our imported oil for both these good reasons-the political reason and the financial reason. But why should the people of my riding, which is as typical a riding as one could find anywhere in Ontario, believe that the government has come to the most viable solution to the energy problems of price and supply? For example, they know that the same government which is offering wholesale nationalization of the Canadian oil and gas industry is the very government which brought the country from a surplus production of 76 million barrels of oil per year in 1974 to a shortfall of 65 million barrels per year in 1978. This will result in compensation payments of $2 billion next year alone. No matter what happens in the way of new strikes of oil, the lead time required for development dictates that one third of our total oil requirement will have to be imported by 1985. This means that even more money will be lifted from the pockets of Peterborough constituents, not just at the gas pumps, even if the pumps display the rather jaunty Petro-Canada maple leaf, but also through their taxes. By 1990 we will be paying up to $9 billion per year for imported oil. This is an alarming figure. It makes up just about 15 per cent of our gross national product. It pretty well takes care of all equalization payments to all provinces on a yearly basis. It goes a long way to servicing our $100 billion national debt. It is four times our largest ever defence contract. In short, it is an unconscionable amount of money to spend on imported oil.
How will our national oil company step in to help the Ontario consumer and taxpayer? What plans does it have for reducing this immense burden? What discount will Canadians enjoy at the pumps for having financed Petro-Canada to the tune of $4 billion?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-48. Along with other members of the New Democratic Party, I have worked to point out the shortcomings and failures of this bill which pretends to usher in a new era of Canadian ownership and Canadian self-sufficiency in our oil and gas industry. My colleagues have shown how the Canadianization provisions are a fraud, and how we are missing the boat by failing to insist upon Canadian content in the spin-off industries. Bill C-48 does not make good economic sense for the Canadian people, although it will make some people very rich. As my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said, it is a matter of privilege triumphing over justice and equity.
However, in addition to opposing the bill on narrow economic terms, New Democrats oppose the bill because it looks to massive petroleum development without proper protection for the environment, or without adequate recognition of the rights of native people. This was symbolized by the failure of the committee to go north and hear directly the first-hand views of those northern people, in spite of having made an earlier promise to do so.
We should always remember that these two factors of Canadian life belong together. We cannot talk about the rights of Indian, Inuit and Metis people without considering their close relationship to the environment, to the land and the water near which they live. Preservation of the environment has to be the bottom line in any genuine concern for the aboriginal peoples of Canada. For these peoples, culture is not a separate, air tight compartment of life that has no relationship to the economy; rather, the culture is completely linked with the economy, and both depend upon the environment. Destroy the environment and one destroys the economy; destroy the economy and one destroys the culture; destroy the culture and one destroys the people.
When we look at reports of the way in which this act will be administered, we understand very well why the aboriginal peoples feel threatened. Although the regulations have not yet been made available, a September 19 report in the Montreal Gazette points out that the administration of oil and gas development in Canada will be handled by the Canada Oil and Gas Lands Administration, or COGLA for short. In theory, COGLA will report both to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and also to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), but the five-member policy committee will have only one member from Indian Affairs and Northern Development and three from Energy, Mines and Resources. No one on that committee will be from the Department of the Environment. No one will be from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. It will be completely dominated by a department that is geared and oriented toward development.
Much of the work of COGLA in determining when, where and how exploration, drilling and production will be carried on will be independent of any other government departments. The
Canada Oil and Gas Act
set-up of COGLA confirms what my colleague the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) meant when he talked about the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development as one of the silent partners of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The other silent partners are the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts). In spite of the massive impact that proposed developments will have on the environment, and in spite of clear hazards to land and water, the Minister of the Environment has remained silent throughout this debate.
My colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller) has pointed to the silence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. For the past ten years we have had a moratorium on offshore exploration and drilling off the coast of British Columbia. Bill C-48 would allow that moratorium to be lifted, with potentially disastrous effects on the west coast fisheries. I ask, where is the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans? Why has he not assured the people of British Columbia that their fisheries will be protected? Why has he not insisted on amendments which would guarantee that protection? The bill fails to provide for mandatory public inquiries into oil spills, and it does not spell out what constitutes an oil spill. All of this is left to the discretion of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He is the man who is in charge of the environment. His track record in regulating, for example, the nuclear industry does not give us any confidence that he will take very good care of the environment as far as petroleum exploration and development are concerned.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development did at least speak on the bill. One of the things he said was that there would be no effect on land claims negotiations. When he appeared before the committee last June, my colleague the hon. member for Skeena asked him the following:
-would you table for this committee a legal opinion that there is no prejudice with the passage of C-48 in relation to aboriginal negotiations and claims, and second, in relation to going from the old regime to the new regime, that negotiations are not precluded by either existing leases or those leases that are to come in the future.
I ask hon. members to note that he very clearly asked the minister to table a legal opinion. The minister replied:
Yes, I can give a legal opinion.
He went on to say:
If you want a legal opinion that states the obvious, I am prepared to try to get that legal opinion for you-sure.
In October the minister was asked about this legal opinion and why he had not tabled it. He replied:
I do not know whether we are arguing about semantics or technicalities. When I mentioned a legal opinion and when I made that statement, 1 meant that I would obtain a view in writing based on a legal opinion I would receive as to what the situation was.
Either the minister has changed his mind about tabling the legal opinion and is not willing to admit it, or he did not understand a basic, straightforward question. In either case, he is failing the Canadian people who expect a little more leadership than that.

November 10, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
We want to see that legal opinion. We believe this legislation does affect land rights. Perhaps what the minister means is that there will be no effect on the minister's prejudiced understanding of those rights and the government's very narrow understanding of what land claims are all about.
If one looks at the policy paper the minister submitted to cabinet last year, it is a very different understanding of what the land claims negotiation is all about than many of the native peoples' understanding when they entered into these negotiations. On page 7 of the document entitled "Discussion Paper: Native Claims Policy-Comprehensive Claims", the minister said:
-the factors which have influenced reaching agreement in particular claims are, among others, the following: first, pressures from the imminence or anticipation of major development in the claimed area-
On page 9 we find this statement:
In respect of priority, efforts should be concentrated on those groups where potential for settlement is most promising and/or urgently required, leaving other groups for the future.
In other words, development will take place, and where development is looked to that is where land claims will be negotiated; but the aboriginal people will have to negotiate with a gun to their head.
Some of the guidelines listed in the annex to that document make clear how poorly the government understands what is needed. First, we find the following:
There must be extinguishment of all land claims based on aboriginal title in exchange for conferral of specific rights and benefits.
The aboriginal people have not wanted extinguishment. What they have fought for and demanded is recognition of their rights. The government is taking the position that yes, it owes them something but the government will only begin to talk about paying that something if the people agree the government does not owe it. The government wants extinguishment. The aboriginal people want recognition.
One of the ways Bill C-48 impacts is clearly spelled out in a recommendation which the minister made about negotiations. He said:
Holders of subsurface rights must have access to native lands where necessary for exploration, development and production of resources, subject to fair compensation as determined through timely negotiation and/or an arbitration
system.
In other words, the Indian people will be handed a situation which they have to accept. They have to conduct their land claims negotiations within those very narrow definitions. For the government to try to maintain that Bill C-48 does not affect land claims negotiations only makes sense in the context of the narrow definition of the government trying to impose what those negotiations should be. It does not make sense in terms of the wider understanding of land claims which the aboriginal people themselves have had. Therefore, it is essential that we should have that legal opinion so that members of this House and the Canadian people can determine what the effect of Bill C-48 will be on aboriginal claims.
Over a year ago members of the Nuu Chah Nulth people on the west coast of Vancouver Island and the Haida people on
the Queen Charlotte Islands submitted aboriginal claims to the minister. To date no answer has been received even as to whether those claims have been accepted for negotiation. Maybe in light of the government's policy of giving priority to areas where there is massive development projected, the people should hope for some kind of offshore drilling. While it would destroy their environment, it would advance the claims process. The government takes a cynical view of waiting for development before pushing ahead with negotiations.
In the minister's speech to the House on October 19, he pointed to the process by which the Norman Wells pipeline was approved. He pointed to that as an example of a balanced approach to the way in which the claims of aboriginal peoples are weighed and looked at as well as the demands of industry. As reported in Hansard at page 11920, the minister said:
This decision was not arrived at lightly. In weighing the elements of the Norman Wells project the government asked the Federal Environmental Review Assessment Office, commonly referred to as FERAO, to consider not just the environmental factors but also the socioeconomic aspects of that project. The National Energy Board also studied the project, and both agencies held public hearings both north and south of 60 and reported positively, subject to specific terms and conditions.
It seems the minister is suggesting that there was an adequate process and the views of the aboriginal people were heard. In the National Energy Board Reasons for Decision, on page 172 we find the following:
As to regional socioeconomic desirability, the Board finds that the proposed pipeline project may not provide the region with a net positive benefit but rather that its modest potential benefits and modest potential liabilities would balance out, at least in the short term.
The National Energy Board is very pro-development. The most the National Energy Board could hope for was that there might be some kind of a trade-off.
The environmental assessment and review process held hearings and reading from page 23 of its report we find:
At most public meetings a representative of the Dene Nation stated the Dene policy position that there should be no development before a land settlement is obtained in the western NWT. In each community, the band chiefs and councillors reinforced this position.
In each community the local spokespeople emphasized that there should be no development without a settlement.

Canada Oil and Gas Act
This bill has a greater effect on small businesses in the oil industry than any other. It does not affect the multinationals because they do not care. It does not hurt the multinationals one iota. If you look at the history of multinationals in various countries you will see that they can increase or decrease their exploration funds as they need. That is not true of the independents, those small oil companies which started up ten or 15 years ago. Yet members of the Liberal party, just as members of the NDP, say they support small business. That is hogwash. They really do not care about small business. Four jobs of every ten are provided by small business. It is laughable when those members opposite tell us they support small business.
Ten or 15 years ago many of these small oil companies just got started. They did not represent very much, but hon. members opposite who remember those days will know where those small businesses went when they wanted funds. Did they go to Toronto or to Montreal? I suggest they did not. Many of them had to go south to get partners. That has been the unfortunate history of this country, supported by the Liberal government. One only has to go back to 1965 when basically these small companies really got started to verify that fact.
Let me now speak directly to the bill. In 1974 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said on a number of occasions that we will have oil self-sufficiency by 1980. We do not have oil self-sufficiency today and there is no possibility we will have it by 1990. The oil companies individually and as a group under IPAC and CPA have told this government there will not be oil self-sufficiency by 1990. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) stands in his place and says: "That is hogwash; of course we will." Then we get a report from the National Energy Board which says we will not have oil selfsufficiency and there is nothing to prove that we will.
At the present time we are consuming approximately 1.8 million barrels a day and we are producing 1.4 million barrels a day. We know our production is decreasing at the rate of
100,000	barrels per day. By 1990 our production will be down to 700,000 barrels per day. The National Energy Board has also confirmed that in 1990 we will still be consuming the same amount of crude oil, namely 1.8 million barrels per day. By 1990 we will need an additional 1.1 million barrels of crude oil per day. Where are we going to find it? Will we find it off the east coast? There is no proven find there presently. We have the possible production of 40,000 or 50,000 barrels a day at the present time, but we have no way of getting the oil out. Are we going to find that additional oil in the Arctic where Dome has just indicated an interesting discovery? Will that account for that 1.1 million barrels deficit in oil? There is little likelihood we will have oil self-sufficiency by 1990. The oil companies have been telling the government this and we have been saying the same, but the government refuses to believe us.
May I call it six o'clock?
